_about: Misconceptions that error items target. home is the lesson whose concept it belongs to; an item in that lesson or a later one is on the path (a later one is a spiral). See AUTHORING.md, Error tasks.

algebra-juxtaposition.text: 2x with x = 4 is read as 24 (the digits side by side) instead of 2 × 4 = 8.

letter-alphabet.text: A letter in a formula is given a value from its place in the alphabet (l = 12); a letter stands for a quantity, whose value is measured or given.

undo-same-operation.text: To find the unknown, the operation in the equation is repeated instead of undone (8 = 2w gives w = 16 instead of w = 4).

reverse-subtract.text: "7 less than n" is written in the order the words are spoken, 7 − n; the amount is taken away from n, so it is n − 7.

missing-brackets.text: "Add 2 to x, then multiply by 6" is written 6x + 2, so the multiplier reaches only the x; the whole x + 2 needs brackets, 6(x + 2).

letter-as-object.text: A letter is read as the object it counts (3a means "3 apples"); a stands for a number, so 3a is 3 times that number.

backtrack-order.text: Steps are undone in the order they were done (divide first in 2x + 3 = 11) instead of last step first.

one-side-only.text: An operation is done to one side of an equation only, which breaks the balance.

m-c-swap.text: The number on its own (c) is read as the steepness, or a bigger m is expected to lift the line instead of making it steeper.

minus-means-down.text: Any minus sign in the rule (such as y = 3x − 2) is taken to mean the line goes down; only a negative m does.

parallel-same-numbers.text: Lines whose rules use the same numbers (y = 2x + 5 and y = 5x + 2) are taken to be parallel; only the same m makes lines parallel.

cross-read-y.text: The y of the point where two lines meet is given as the solution; the solution is its x (the y is the value of both sides there).

fee-decides.text: The plan with the lower starting fee is taken to be cheaper for every amount; which plan is cheaper changes where the lines cross.

pattern-scaling.text: Figure 10 of a growing pattern is taken to be 10 copies of Figure 1 (4 × 10 = 40); shared parts mean each figure adds less than Figure 1 has.

pair-order.text: An ordered pair is written output first, (11, 4) for x = 4 and y = 11, or the same number is used for both; the input comes first, (4, 11).

plot-up-first.text: A point (x, y) is plotted by going up x and across y; across comes first, then up.

variable-copies-later.text: Storing a new value in a name changes lines that already ran; in fact a line uses the value the name holds when it runs, so only later lines change.

counter-constant.text: The loop counter i is the same number on every pass; in fact it is 0 on the first pass, 1 on the second, and so on.

update-is-equation.text: size = size + 5 is impossible because nothing equals itself plus 5; in fact = means store: work out the right side, then store the answer in the name.

update-outside-loop.text: An update line placed after a loop still grows the value on every pass; in fact only an indented line runs on each pass, and one after the loop runs once.

turn-draws.text: right(90) moves the turtle 90 steps or draws something; in fact it only turns the turtle on the spot, and only forward draws.

order-free.text: The same lines in any order draw the same picture; in fact the commands run top to bottom and each turn changes which way the next forward goes.

loop-body-indent.text: A loop repeats only its first line, or everything after it; in fact it repeats exactly the lines indented under it.

count-wrong-variable.text: A loop's count is taken from a variable that happens to have the right value (range(houses) for a square's 4 sides); it works only until that variable changes.

angle-from-sides.text: The turn is guessed or multiplied instead of worked out as 360 / sides.

assign-vs-compare.text: A single = is used to ask whether two things are equal.

list-index-range.text: A list of n items has a place n; places run from 0 to n - 1.

name-rebinding.text: Defining (or importing) a name twice keeps both; in fact the later one silently replaces the earlier.

copied-code.text: Copying working code is free; in fact every copy must be fixed separately.

return-vs-print.text: print gives a value back; only return does, and a function without return gives None.

handler-call-vs-pass.text: Handing over a handler with brackets calls it at once instead of passing the function.

global-missing.text: A function can change a variable made outside it just by assigning to it, without a global line.

text-plus-number.text: + can join a number straight onto text; in fact the number must become text first, with str().

input-is-text.text: input() gives back a number when digits are typed; in fact it is always text until int() turns it into a number.

loop-never-changes.text: A while loop ends by itself; in fact something inside it must change what the condition tests, or it runs for ever.

dot-missing.text: A command without a name in front goes to the turtle you meant; in fact it goes to the default turtle.

parallel-lists-sync.text: Lists that describe the same things stay in step by themselves; in fact every list must be changed together.

dict-key-quotes.text: A dictionary key works without quotes; in fact star[speed] looks for a variable called speed.

self-missing.text: speed = speed inside __init__ stores the value in the object; in fact only self.speed = speed does.

method-self.text: A method needs no parameter for the object; in fact Python passes the object as self, so def move(self) needs it.

text-case.text: Text compares equal whatever its capitals; in fact "Yes" == "yes" is False.

remove-missing.text: remove() does nothing when the item is not in the list; in fact it stops with a ValueError.

key-exact.text: A dictionary finds a key that is nearly the same; in fact the key must match exactly, capitals included.

csv-text-values.text: Values read from a CSV file are numbers when they look like numbers; in fact every value is text until int() or float() changes it.

total-replaced.text: total = value adds the value on; in fact it replaces the total, so only the last value is kept.

count-key-missing.text: counts[key] + 1 works the first time a key turns up; in fact the key must exist first, so a new key has to start at 1.

route-missing.text: Any function in a Flask app is a page; in fact only a function with an @app.route line above it answers an address.

template-vars.text: A template can use any variable in the program; in fact it sees only the values passed to render_template_string by name.

form-name-attr.text: A form sends each box under its id; in fact only boxes with a name attribute are sent, under that name.

write-mode-append.text: Opening a file with "w" adds to the end of it; in fact "w" empties it first, and "a" adds to the end.

call-parens.text: Writing a function's name runs it; in fact load_members is the function itself, and load_members() runs it and gives its result.

query-text.text: A number in a web address arrives as a number; in fact it is text unless the parameter's type (age: int) converts it.

inputs-order.text: Gradio matches inputs to parameters by name or label; in fact it passes them in order, the first input to the first parameter.

return-missing-value.text: A function gives back every variable it works out; in fact it gives back only what follows return, so each output needs a value there.

return-in-loop.text: A return inside a loop waits until the loop finishes; in fact return ends the function at once, on the first time round.

nested-level.text: A value deep inside nested dictionaries can be looked up with its own key straight away; in fact each level needs its own [key], from the outside in.

compare-direction.text: > keeps the smallest value so far; in fact > keeps the biggest, and < keeps the smallest.

test-on-train.text: Testing a model on the data it learned from shows how good it is; in fact it must be tested on data it has not seen.

feature-order.text: A model knows which number is which measurement; in fact it reads them by position, so they must be in the same order as in training.

open-w-reads.text: open(name, "w") opens a file to read it; in fact "w" empties the file at once, ready for writing.

except-any.text: except catches any error; in fact except ValueError catches only a ValueError, and other errors still stop the program.

and-vs-or.text: Conditions that must all hold are joined with or instead of and.

html-error-message.text: A mistake in HTML stops the page with an error message, as in Python; the browser actually shows its best guess and says nothing.

tag-overlap.text: Tags can close in any order, so they overlap (…) instead of nesting.

list-item-outside.text: An <li> works anywhere, not only inside a <ul> or <ol>.

table-row-cells.text: A row can have fewer cells than the others, and the browser lines the table up anyway.

selector-mismatch.text: A rule styles an element even when its selector does not exactly match the tag or class (a typo, or a class without its dot).

css-missing-unit.text: A size works without a unit, as in padding: 10.

flex-on-items.text: display: flex goes on the items to line them up, instead of on the box that holds them.

label-not-linked.text: A label belongs to the input next to it, whatever its for says.

img-file-name.text: The browser finds a picture from a name close to the real file name; the name, extension and capitals must match exactly.

semantic-tags-look.text: Section tags such as header and footer change how a page looks or where things go; they only name the parts, and CSS decides the look.

grid-on-items.text: display: grid and its columns go on each item, instead of on the box that holds them.

blocks-show-together.text: All the blocks in on start show at once (or only the first does); in fact they run one at a time from the top, each picture replacing the last.

run-once-vs-forever.text: Blocks in on start keep running; in fact they run once and the last picture stays.

pause-ends-loop.text: A pause inside forever stops the loop; in fact it only holds the picture for that long, then forever carries on.

button-check-once.text: Checking a button in on start watches for presses; in fact it checks once, at the start, before anyone presses.

event-runs-at-start.text: The blocks inside an event run when the micro:bit starts; in fact they wait and run only when that event happens.

reset-in-loop.text: Setting a variable's start value inside forever is harmless; in fact it resets the variable again and again, wiping every change.

change-replaces.text: change count by 1 sets count to 1; in fact it adds 1 to whatever count is now, while set replaces it.

comparison-direction.text: < and > can be read either way round, so the condition is true in the opposite case to the one intended.

if-false-undoes.text: When an if's question becomes false, it undoes what it did; in fact a false if does nothing at all, so turning something off needs its own question.

else-runs-too.text: The else part runs after the if part as well; in fact exactly one of the two parts runs each time.

else-if-order.text: Every else if is checked; in fact the first true question wins, so a wider question asked first hides the narrower ones after it.

list-first-is-one.text: The first item of a list is at place 1; in fact places start at 0, so the last is the length minus 1.

last-place-is-length.text: The last place of a list of 3 items is 3; in fact places start at 0, so it is 2.

pick-range-fixed.text: pick random 0 to 2 works for any list; in fact a fixed range never reaches items added later, so pick 0 to length − 1.

define-not-call.text: Making a function runs it; in fact its blocks only run when something calls it.

copied-blocks.text: Copying blocks to a second place is free; in fact every copy must be kept the same by hand, which a function avoids.

radio-group-mismatch.text: Any micro:bit nearby hears a radio message; in fact only micro:bits in the same group receive it.

hears-own-message.text: A micro:bit receives its own radio message; in fact only the other micro:bits in the group receive it.

one-handler-per-message.text: Each number sent needs its own on radio received block; in fact one block receives every message, and receivedNumber says which one arrived.

shared-code-mismatch.text: Each micro:bit can order its list of words its own way; in fact both must share the same list in the same order, because only the place number is sent.

running-time-from-press.text: running time counts from the moment you press a button; in fact it counts from when the micro:bit started, so a time between is one reading minus another.

flag-never-reset.text: Setting a true/false variable once is enough; in fact it must be set back, or it keeps saying true and every later press counts.

screen-y-up.text: y counts up from the bottom, as in maths; in fact the screen y counts down from the top, so a bigger y is lower.

moves-to-numbers.text: The numbers in move with buttons are a place to go to; in fact they are speeds across and down, so a 0 stops that direction.

controller-any-sprite.text: Every sprite answers the arrow keys; in fact only the sprite named in move with buttons does.

position-vs-velocity.text: Setting a speed moves a sprite once, like setting its position; in fact velocity keeps moving it every frame until something changes it.

kind-mismatch.text: Any two sprites that touch run an overlap event; in fact only the two kinds named in the event do, so a sprite made with the wrong kind is never noticed.

overlap-repeats.text: An overlap event runs once per touch; in fact it runs every frame the sprites still touch, unless one is destroyed or moved.

game-over-needs-block.text: A game needs a game over block to end when the lives run out; in fact Info ends the game by itself at 0 lives.

timer-runs-once.text: A timer event runs once, after its wait; in fact it runs again and again, every so many milliseconds, for the whole game.

random-picked-once.text: pick random chooses once, so every rock gets the same height; in fact it picks again each time the block runs.

check-in-start.text: An if in on start keeps watching the game; in fact it is asked once, before the game begins.

chase-sign.text: Which way a chaser should move can be read either way round, so the speed gets the wrong sign and the chaser moves away from the player.

projectile-kind.text: A projectile is the player that fired it; in fact it is its own kind (Projectile), so a Player–Enemy overlap never notices a hit.

loop-runs-once.text: A block in a for element loop runs once; in fact it runs once for each item in the list, so it reaches every sprite of the kind.

arcade-define-not-call.text: Making a function runs it; in fact its blocks only run when something calls it.

param-fixed-inside.text: To change what a function does for one call, change the number inside the function; in fact that changes every call, and the call's own value is what should change.

gravity-steady-speed.text: Gravity makes a sprite fall at a steady speed; in fact ay adds to vy every second, so it falls faster and faster.

jump-midair.text: A jump only needs a speed upwards; without a check that the sprite is on the ground, every press jumps again, even in the air.

update-fires-every-frame.text: An if in on game update fires once when it becomes true; in fact it fires every frame while it stays true.

arcade-list-first-is-one.text: The first item of a list is at place 1; in fact places start at 0, so level 0 reads the first item.

flag-never-reset-arcade.text: Setting a true/false variable is enough for a power-up to end; in fact it stays as it is until a block sets it back.

count-below-zero.text: Taking one away each time is enough to limit a power-up; in fact without a check first the count goes below zero and never stops anything.

overlap-not-collision.text: Touching sprites push each other, like objects; in fact an overlap is only an event, so sprites pass through each other unless your blocks move them.

timed-move-stops.text: A move with a time (for 1000 ms) stops when the time is up; in fact the motors keep going until another motor block changes them.

line-steer-wrong-way.text: When a line sensor sees the line, steer away from it; in fact a sensor on the line means the line is on that side, so steer towards it.

music-background-no-wait.text: Music played in the background finishes before the next block runs; in fact the program moves on at once, so the next cue is sent straight away.

alert-repeats.text: A message sent in forever when something happens is sent once; in fact it is sent again every time round while it stays true.

axes-swapped.text: The number read up the side is taken as the one measured along the bottom, or the two values of a point are swapped; in fact each number belongs to its own axis, named in the axis label.

graph-as-picture.text: A graph is read as a picture of the journey or the object, so a line going down means going downhill; in fact it shows how one measurement changes with another.

negative-magnitude.text: Negatives are compared by their size without the sign (−8 > −2 because 8 > 2); on a number line −8 is further left, so it is less.

subtract-negative.text: The minus sign of the number is taken as the move (5 − (−3): move left 3, giving 2); subtracting moves the opposite way to adding, so subtracting −3 moves right 3, giving 8.

angle-sum-size.text: A bigger triangle has bigger angles, so its angle sum is more than 180°; enlarging a triangle changes its sides, not its angles, and every triangle's angles add to 180°.

polygon-centre-angles.text: A polygon split from a point in the middle into n triangles has angle sum n × 180°; that counts the full turn of 360° around the middle point, which is not an angle of the polygon.

negative-decimal-direction.text: The part after the whole number of a negative decimal or mixed numeral is counted back towards zero (−1.5 placed halfway between −1 and 0); it is further from zero too, so −1.5 is halfway between −2 and −1.

partial-distribution.text: The number outside a bracket multiplies only the first term (4(x + 3) = 4x + 3); it multiplies every term inside, so 4x + 12.

hcf-not-highest.text: A common factor that is not the highest is taken out (12x − 8 = 2(6x − 4)); the bracket still shares a factor, so it is not fully factorised: 4(3x − 2).

divide-one-term.text: Only one term of a side is divided when rearranging (y = 4x − 3 becomes y ÷ 4 = x − 3); dividing a side divides every term, so undo the − 3 first: x = (y + 3)/4.

vertically-opposite-pair.text: A pair at one crossing (vertically opposite, such as b and c) is called alternate or corresponding; the parallel-line pairs take one angle at each crossing.

co-interior-equal.text: Co-interior angles are taken to be equal, like alternate and corresponding angles; they add to 180°.

assume-equal-angles.text: Two angles that look related are taken as a named pair (b and e called alternate) without a rule that links them; every step needs a named rule, so find an angle in between.

wrong-angle-sum.text: The triangle's 180° is used for a quadrilateral (or another polygon); the angle sum depends on the number of sides: (n − 2) × 180°, so 360° for a quadrilateral.

fraction-add-same.text: The same number is added to the top and the bottom to make an equal fraction (2/3 = 3/4); that changes the amount, so multiply or divide both by the same number.

decimal-percent-place.text: The digits after the point are read as the percentage (0.5 = 5%); 0.5 is 50 hundredths, so 50%: multiply a decimal by 100.

inverse-sign.text: A term is removed by doing what its sign shows instead of the inverse (taking 7 away to undo − 7); undo − 7 by adding 7 to both sides.

boundary-solid.text: The boundary of a strict inequality (< or >) is drawn solid; its points make the two sides equal, so they are not included: dashed. Solid is for ≤ and ≥.

inequality-reverse.text: The inequality sign is kept when both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative (−2x > 6 gives x > −3); multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the order, so x < −3.

discrete-decimal.text: Any data with decimals is taken to be continuous (shoe sizes 7.5, prices); data that can only take separate values is discrete, and continuous data is measured, so it can take any value in a range.

median-unsorted.text: The median is taken as the middle of the list as written; the values must be sorted first.

mean-always-best.text: The mean is taken as always the best average because it uses every value; an outlier pulls it away from the typical values, so with one the median is usually better.

stem-skip-empty.text: Stems with no leaves are left out of a stem-and-leaf plot; every stem from the smallest to the largest belongs in it, or gaps in the data are hidden.

compare-single-value.text: Two data sets are compared by a single value (the highest score); a fair comparison uses a measure of centre and a measure of spread for each set.

equally-likely-outcomes.text: Every outcome in the sample space is taken to be equally likely (three colours, so 1/3 each); favourable ÷ total only works when they are, otherwise use the sizes or counts.

expect-exact.text: The expected count is expected to happen exactly, so a small difference in a short experiment is taken as proof of unfairness; results vary around the expected count, more so in few trials.

gamblers-fallacy.text: After a run of one outcome, the other is thought more likely (the coin is due a head); each trial is independent, and the relative frequency settles because of many more trials, not by balancing out.

sign-rules-addition.text: The addition rule is used for multiplying (−4 × (−3) = −12, "two negatives make a bigger negative"); for multiplying and dividing, the same signs give a positive.

square-double.text: 5² is read as 5 × 2 = 10 (and a square root as halving: √36 = 18); squaring multiplies a number by itself: 5 × 5 = 25.

power-times.text: 2⁵ is read as 2 × 5 = 10; the exponent counts how many 2s are multiplied: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.

tree-stops-early.text: A factor tree is stopped at a number that is not prime (4 or 9), so the factorisation is not all primes: 36 = 4 × 9 is not 2² × 3².

lcm-product.text: The product of two numbers is taken as their lowest common multiple (6 × 8 = 48); when they share a prime, the LCM is lower: 24.

fraction-add-across.text: The tops and the bottoms are added (1/3 + 1/4 = 2/7); parts of different sizes cannot be counted together until both are cut into the same parts: 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.

multiply-makes-bigger.text: Multiplying is thought always to make a number bigger (and dividing smaller); multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes it smaller: 1/2 × 8 = 4.

decrease-multiplier.text: To decrease by 20%, the amount is multiplied by 0.2 (the part taken off) instead of 0.8 (what is left), so the answer is the discount, not the new price.

slant-height.text: The slanted side is used as the height (7 × 5 for base 7, slanted side 5, height 4); the height is the perpendicular distance from the base, at a right angle to it.

triangle-no-half.text: A triangle's area is taken as base × height without halving; that is the area of the parallelogram two copies make.

area-units.text: Lengths in different units are multiplied without converting (2 m × 50 cm = 100), or the area is given in cm instead of cm²; area counts squares, and both lengths must be in the same unit.

volume-visible-cubes.text: Only the cubes that can be seen in a picture are counted (or the faces are added, a surface area); a prism is full of cubes, layer under layer: base area × height.

radius-diameter.text: The radius and the diameter are mixed up (a radius of 5 read as a diameter of 5); the diameter is two radii, right across through the centre.

pi-exact.text: π is taken to be exactly 3.14 or 22/7; π is a fixed number that never ends or repeats (3.14159…), and 3.14 and 22/7 are approximations.

score-set.text: score = 1 adds one to the score; in fact it sets the score to 1 every time, so it never goes higher. score += 1 adds one.

key-always-there.text: keyboard.LEFT can be asked about from the first frame; in fact microStudio adds it only after the first key press, so the game stops with an AttributeError until then.

acute-one-angle.text: A triangle is called acute because it has an acute angle (every triangle has at least two); an acute triangle has all three angles less than 90°, and one angle over 90° makes it obtuse.

square-not-rectangle.text: A square is said not to be a rectangle (or a rhombus) because its sides are all equal; a square has every property of a rectangle, so it is a special rectangle.

regular-sides-only.text: A polygon with equal sides is called regular even when its angles differ (a rhombus); regular needs equal sides and equal angles.

pyth-no-squares.text: The two shorter sides are added to give the hypotenuse (6 + 8 = 14); it is their squares that add (36 + 64 = 100), so c = √100 = 10.

pyth-add-for-leg.text: A shorter side is found by adding the squares (b² = 10² + 6²), which gives a side longer than the hypotenuse; for a shorter side, subtract: b² = 10² − 6².

c-not-longest.text: The theorem is tested with any side as c (5² + 13² against 12²); c must be the longest side, so test 5² + 12² against 13².

function-case.text: A function's name can be typed with any capitals; in fact drawFlower and drawflower are different names, so the call must match the definition exactly.

near-is-small.text: A touch is when the distance is big; in fact two things touch when the distance between them is small, so the test is dist(...) < 20, not > 20.

selector-typo.text: A selector that is nearly right still finds the element; in fact it must match the id or class exactly, or the browser finds nothing (null) and the next line fails.

selector-prefix.text: querySelector("title") finds the element with id title; in fact a bare word means a tag, an id needs # and a class needs a dot.

script-order.text: A script can sit anywhere in the page; in fact it runs as soon as the browser reaches it, so an element below it does not exist yet and querySelector finds null.

call-not-pass.text: addEventListener("click", show()) runs show when the button is clicked; in fact show() runs straight away, once, and the event gets its answer. Give it the name: show.

class-dot.text: classList.add(".dark") needs the dot as in CSS; in fact classList takes the plain class name, dark.

value-is-text.text: An input's value is a number when the person types a number; in fact it is always text, so "2" + "3" is "23". Number(input.value) makes it a number.

list-is-live.text: Changing the array changes the list on the page; in fact the page only changes when the code makes or removes elements. Update the array and the page.

state-in-handler.text: A variable made inside the click function keeps its value from click to click; in fact it is made again each time, so it starts over. Make it above the function.

name-typo.text: A variable name that is nearly right still works; in fact count and cout are different names, and JavaScript says the second is not defined.

fill-after.text: fill colours the shapes already on the canvas; in fact it only colours shapes drawn after it, so fill above the shape, not below.

let-in-draw.text: A variable made with let inside draw() keeps its value from one frame to the next; in fact it is made again, at its starting value, every frame, so the shape never moves.

assign-in-if.text: A single = in an if asks whether two things are equal; in fact it sets the variable to the value (and is then always true), and === asks.

y-from-top.text: A bar's y is its bottom edge, so y = its height stands it on the bottom; in fact y is the top edge and counts down, so a bar standing on the bottom has its top at the canvas height minus its height.

property-prefix.text: Inside the loop, speed on its own is the star's speed; in fact it is a name p5 does not know, and the star's speed is star.speed.

power-off-by-one.text: The exponent for a place value column is counted from 1 at the ones (tens as 10², hundreds as 10³); the ones column is 10⁰, so every power is one too big.

round-truncate.text: A decimal is rounded by cutting digits off (3.789 to 2 places as 3.78); look at the next digit, and if it is 5 or more, round up (3.79).

round-double.text: Rounding is done twice, digit by digit (2.349 to 1 place: 2.35 then 2.4); only the digit straight after the place matters, so 2.349 rounds to 2.3.

est-zero-slip.text: An estimate is rounded to the wrong size (19.6 × 4.1 as 2 × 4 = 8); round to the leading digit and keep its size: 20 × 4 = 80.

ratio-part-whole.text: A ratio of one part to the whole is written as part to part (2 red and 3 blue: red to all the counters written 2 : 3); part to whole is 2 : 5.

ratio-add-not-multiply.text: An equivalent ratio is made by adding the same number to both terms (2 : 3 = 4 : 5); multiply or divide both terms by the same number: 2 : 3 = 4 : 6.

share-by-term.text: A total is shared in a ratio by dividing it by each term ($60 in 2 : 3 as 60 ÷ 2 and 60 ÷ 3); add the terms to find the parts, then divide the total by the number of parts.

model-no-units.text: A solution is given as a bare number from the calculator; say what it means in the situation, with its units and sensible rounding.

est-no-compare.text: The estimate is made but not compared with the calculator's answer by size (10.227 called close to 100); an answer is reasonable only if it is near the estimate.

percent-wrong-base.text: A percentage profit or change is found out of the new amount (profit $3 on a $5 cost sold for $8 as 3 ÷ 8 = 37.5%); it is out of the original: 3 ÷ 5 = 60%.

net-count-only.text: A net with six squares is said to fold into a cube because a cube has six faces (a 2 × 3 block, or six in a row); the squares must also land on six different faces, so fold it or roll a cube over it.

view-adds-up.text: A view is found by adding every pile in a column; a front or side view shows only the tallest pile in each column, so lower cubes behind it are hidden.

translate-sign.text: A move left or down is added to the coordinate (4 left on x = 2 gives 6); left and down take away: 2 − 4 = −2.

reflect-axis-swap.text: The coordinate that changes sign is chosen by the axis's direction (the x-axis is horizontal, so x changes); a reflection in the x-axis changes y, because the point moves up or down across the mirror.

rotate-swap-only.text: A quarter turn about the origin is said to just swap the coordinates, (3, 1) to (1, 3); the swap also changes one sign, and the direction decides which: (x, y) to (−y, x) anticlockwise.

algo-general-first.text: An algorithm tests the wider property first (two pairs of parallel sides) so a rectangle or square is given the less specific name; test the most specific class first, or the tests must be ordered so each shape reaches its own name.

vary-two-at-once.text: Two variables are changed together to test the effect of one (h and w both changed in V = lwh); only a change to one variable at a time shows which letter caused the change in the output.

sample-generalise.text: A result from a few friendly or convenient people is stated for the whole group (8 swimmers become all of Year 7); the report must say who was measured and how they were chosen.

composite-wrong-height.text: A piece of a composite shape is given the whole shape's height or width (the 5 m wide part of an L taken as 6 m tall); each piece uses its own lengths.

estimate-part-full.text: Every grid square an irregular shape touches is counted as a whole square, so the estimate is too big; part squares count as half each.

cube-conversion.text: A cubic unit is converted with the length factor once (1 m³ = 100 cm³); it is used three times: 1 m³ = 100 × 100 × 100 = 1 000 000 cm³.

prism-lwh-always.text: Length × width × height is used for every prism (a triangular prism with legs 3 and 4 and length 10 as 120); the volume is the end's area times the length (60).

circle-area-circumference.text: The circumference formula 2πr is used for the area of a circle; the area is πr², in square units.

circle-forget-root.text: When finding the radius from an area, A ÷ π is taken as the radius; it is r², so a square root is still needed.

tz-wrong-direction.text: The difference between time zones is added for a place that is behind (a smaller offset); a smaller offset means an earlier time, so take it away.

recurring-is-irrational.text: A decimal that goes on forever is called irrational (1/7 = 0.142857…); a decimal that repeats is a fraction, so it is rational. Only decimals that never stop and never repeat are irrational.

terminate-no-simplify.text: The terminating rule is applied before simplifying (3/12 said to recur because 12 has a 3); 3/12 = 1/4, so it terminates.

root-always-irrational.text: Every square root is called irrational (√16 included); the root of a perfect square is a whole number, so it is rational.

root-as-half.text: A square root is found by halving (√50 about 25); it is the number that times itself gives 50, so √50 is just over 7.

index-multiply-base.text: The bases are multiplied as well as the indices added (3² × 3⁴ = 9⁶); the base stays the same: 3⁶.

index-different-bases.text: The index laws are used on powers of different bases (2³ × 3² = 6⁵); they only join powers of the same base.

tax-whole-income.text: The whole income is taxed at the rate of its top bracket; each part of the income is taxed at its own bracket's rate.

rate-inverted.text: A unit rate is found by dividing the wrong way (3 kg for $12 gives 3 ÷ 12 = $0.25 per kg); dollars per kilogram is dollars ÷ kilograms: $4 per kg.

rate-multiply-divide.text: Distance is multiplied by speed to find a time (150 × 60); the units show time = distance ÷ speed: 150 ÷ 60 = 2.5 h.

model-round-down.text: A model's answer is rounded to the nearest whole number when the situation needs rounding up (2.4 L of paint as 2 tins); 2 tins are not enough, so buy 3.

model-blame-maths.text: A model's mismatch with real life is blamed on correct arithmetic; the cause is an assumption that did not hold, such as a steady speed with no stops.

ssa-is-test.text: Two sides and any angle are taken as SAS; SAS needs the angle between the two sides, and two sides with an angle not between them (SSA) can make two different triangles.

similar-add.text: An enlarged side is found by adding the same amount to every side (4, 6 become 7, 9); similar shapes multiply every length by the same scale factor.

proof-by-picture.text: A property is taken as proved because it looks true in one drawing or on one measured example; a proof gives reasons (such as a congruence test) that hold for every shape of the kind.

opp-angles-supplementary.text: A parallelogram's opposite angles are taken to add to 180°; opposite angles are equal, and it is neighbouring (co-interior) angles that add to 180°.

coord3d-order.text: The coordinates of a point in 3D are written in the order they were read, or with the height first; the order is always (x, y, z), so up is the third number.

complement-exclusive.text: Two events that cannot happen together are called complementary (rolling a 1 and rolling a 6); complementary events must also cover every outcome, so P(B) is not 1 − P(A) unless they do.

venn-double-count.text: A group's whole total is written in the 'only' part of a Venn diagram (22 like tea written as tea only), so the overlap is counted twice; write both first and take it from each total.

pairs-order.text: Outcomes that differ only in order are listed once (HH, TT, one of each), so the sample space is too small and unequal outcomes look equally likely; HT and TH are different outcomes.

or-double-count.text: P(A or B) is found by adding P(A) and P(B), counting the outcomes in both twice; take the overlap away once.

sim-too-few.text: A short simulation's result is taken as the probability (no 12 in 20 rolls of two dice, so P(12) = 0); a few trials vary a lot, so compare with the sample space and run many more.

census-always.text: A census is taken to be always the best way to collect data because it is exact; when measuring destroys the item, costs too much or takes too long, a sample is the sensible choice.

big-sample-no-bias.text: A very large sample is taken to be unbiased (1200 phone-in votes must be right); size reduces chance error, but a self-selected or convenience sample stays biased however big it is.

random-haphazard.text: Picking people yourself without a plan is called random; random means every member has the same chance, through a hat, dice or a random number generator.

sample-is-population.text: A sample's mean or proportion is reported as the population's exact value; it is an estimate, given with the sampling method and size.

sample-differ-wrong.text: Two fair samples that give different results are taken to mean one is wrong; random samples hold different members, so they vary by chance (sampling variation).

infer-beyond-population.text: A sample from one group (one school, one class) is used to make claims about a bigger population (all teenagers); an inference is only about the population the sample was drawn from.

binary-place-reversed.text: Binary places are counted from the left (1, 2, 4, 8), so 1100 is read as 3; the 1 place is on the right, so 1100 is 8 + 4 = 12.

binary-max-forgets-zero.text: n bits make 2ⁿ patterns, so the largest number is taken to be 2ⁿ (4 bits up to 16); one pattern is 0, so the largest is 2ⁿ − 1.

data-meaning-fixed.text: Stored numbers are taken to have one fixed meaning (72, 105, 33 are the word Hi!); the meaning comes from the encoding a program reads them with, so a paint program shows the same numbers as greys.

digit-char-code.text: A digit in text is stored as its value (the 7 in "Year 7" as 7); in text a digit is a character with its own code (7 is 55).

light-mixes-like-paint.text: Screen colours are mixed like paint (red and green make brown); a screen adds light, so 255, 255, 0 is yellow.

sound-stored-as-wave.text: A recording is thought to store the sound wave's shape exactly; it stores samples, measurements at regular times rounded to levels, so it is close but not exact.

or-means-not-both.text: OR is read as everyday "one or the other, not both" (1 OR 1 = 0); OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1. One but not both is XOR.

char-one-bit.text: Each character is taken to be one bit (cat is 3 bits); one bit has only two values, so a character code needs a byte, 8 bits.

rle-start-white.text: A row that starts black is coded from its first run (black black white… as 2, 6); the first count is always white, so it starts with 0: 0, 2, 6.

lossy-recoverable.text: Detail thrown away by lossy compression is thought to be restored when the file is opened; it was never stored, so it is gone for good.

bs-modifier-alone.text: A Bootstrap colour class such as btn-primary styles a button on its own; in fact the look comes from the base class (btn) and btn-primary only changes its colour, so a button needs both.

bs-made-up-class.text: Any sensible class name works in Bootstrap (column, blue-button); in fact only the names in its stylesheet do anything, and a wrong one is silently ignored.

bs-order.text: Your own CSS always beats Bootstrap's; in fact when two rules match equally, the later one wins, so your <style> goes after the Bootstrap link.

vue-plain-variable.text: Any variable returned from setup keeps the page up to date; in fact Vue watches only data made with ref (or computed), so a plain let variable changes without the page knowing.

vue-for-parent.text: v-for on the <ul> makes one <li> per item; in fact v-for repeats the tag it is written on, so it goes on the <li>.

vue-value-in-script.text: In the script a ref works like the value inside it (score++); in fact the value is score.value. The page unwraps refs for you; the script does not.

vue-derived-once.text: A total worked out from data in setup stays up to date; in fact a plain calculation runs once, so a value that depends on data belongs in computed().

vue-prop-colon.text: score="p.score" passes the value of p.score; in fact without the colon it passes the words p.score, so use :score to pass a value.

react-mutate.text: In React or Preact, changing an array and passing it back to setItems updates the page; in fact it compares the old and new arrays, sees the same one and skips the update, so pass a new array ([...items, name]).

fetch-no-await.text: fetch and response.json() give the data straight away; in fact each gives a promise (a value that arrives later), so await each one before using it.

bandwidth-is-latency.text: More bandwidth is thought to make each packet arrive sooner, so a faster plan fixes lag; bandwidth is how much data a second, latency is the delay for each packet.

resend-whole-message.text: A lost packet is thought to mean resending the whole message; with TCP only the packet that was never acknowledged is sent again.

packets-private.text: A message is thought to be seen only by its receiver; its packets pass through Wi-Fi, routers and networks others control, and anyone there can copy plain text.

encrypt-at-router.text: Data is thought to be encrypted by the router or the network; it is encrypted on the device (HTTPS) before it leaves, or the first hop would expose it.

bigger-gear-faster.text: A bigger gear is thought to turn faster; a bigger driven gear turns slower, because more of its teeth must be pushed past for each turn.

gear-ratio-upside-down.text: The gear ratio is worked out as driver ÷ driven; it is driven ÷ driver, so swapping the gears makes the output faster and weaker, not stronger.

gear-one-effect.text: A gear ratio is thought to change only the speed or only the force; it changes both, by the same factor in opposite directions.

storage-text-only.text: localStorage keeps a list as a list; in fact it keeps only text, so save a list with JSON.stringify and load it with JSON.parse.

heading-for-size.text: A heading level is chosen by how big it looks (an h4 because it is small); in fact headings are the page's outline, read out by screen readers in order, so go h1, h2, h3 and set the size with CSS.

path-from-my-computer.text: A path that works on my computer (C:\Users\…\trophy.svg or /Users/…) works on the web; in fact the site only has its own folder, so use a relative path such as trophy.svg.

apps-talk-to-hardware.text: Apps are thought to talk to hardware directly, so new hardware needs new apps; apps ask the operating system, which uses a driver for each device.

lookalike-domain.text: A name that looks like a known site is trusted (schoo1 for school); DNS looks up the exact name, so a lookalike reaches a different computer.

signed-in-means-allowed.text: Signing in is taken to allow anything; authentication proves who you are, and permissions (authorisation) decide what you may do.

hash-reversible.text: A stored password hash is thought to be turned back into the password (to email it, for example); a hash is one way, which is why sites send a reset link instead.

counter-in-loop.text: A counter set to 0 inside the loop keeps adding up; in fact it goes back to 0 every time round, so set it to 0 once, before the loop.

one-wire-enough.text: One wire from a pin is thought to be enough to light an LED, as if the pin pushes power one way; current only flows around a complete loop back to GND.

resistor-before-led.text: The resistor is thought to have to come before the LED to protect it; in a single loop the current is the same everywhere, so it works on either side.

floating-pin-reads-zero.text: A pin joined to nothing is thought to read 0; it floats, picks up noise and reads 0 or 1 at random, so a pull-down (or pull-up) resistor holds it.

reading-is-volts.text: An analog reading is thought to be the volts on the pin; it is a number from 0 to 1023 standing for 0 to 3.3 V.

code-any-pin.text: The code is thought to work whatever pin the part is wired to; the pin number in the code must match the pin the wire goes to.

setup-repeats.text: Code in setup() is thought to run again and again; setup() runs once when the board starts, and only loop() repeats.

cpp-assign-in-if.text: A single = in an if is thought to compare; in C++ it sets the variable (and the if then uses that value), so == is needed to compare.

cpp-plus-joins-text.text: "words" + a number is thought to join them, as in Python; in C++ it moves along the text, so print the words and the number separately.

pwm-lower-voltage.text: analogWrite is thought to give the pin a lower voltage; the pin switches fully on and off very fast, and the value sets how much of the time it is on.

analog-range-mismatch.text: A reading is passed straight to an output with a different range; analogRead gives 0 to 1023 but analogWrite takes 0 to 255, so scale it (divide by 4).

ram-is-storage.text: RAM and storage are thought to be one "memory" (8 GB RAM + 256 GB storage = 264 GB of memory); RAM is the working space that empties when the power goes off, storage is what the computer keeps.

storage-size-is-speed.text: A bigger drive is thought to be a faster one; size (GB, TB) is how much it holds, and its type (SSD or HDD) decides how fast it reads.

biggest-spec-best.text: The option with the biggest numbers is thought to be best for every job; a spec only helps when that part is the job's bottleneck.

breadboard-rows.text: The holes along a lettered row are thought to be joined; on a breadboard each numbered column's five holes (a–e, or f–j) are joined, and the gap separates the halves.

tests-skip-boundary.text: A design is tested only with values far from the threshold; the slips are at the boundary (299, 300, 301), so test there too.

pico-same-numbers.text: Numbers are thought to carry straight over from Arduino to MicroPython; time.sleep takes seconds, not milliseconds, and the Pico's read_u16 gives 0 to 65535, not 0 to 1023.

gate-reads-switches.text: Every gate in a circuit is taken to use the switches; each gate uses only what arrives on its own wires, often another gate's output.

binary-digit-two.text: 1 + 1 is written as 2 in a binary sum; binary has only 0 and 1, so 1 + 1 = 10: write 0, carry 1.

latch-forgets.text: A latch is thought to work like a lamp, dropping back to 0 when Set goes off; with Set and Reset both off it keeps its last value, which is what makes it memory.

code-not-numbers.text: Instructions and data are thought to be different kinds of thing in memory; instructions are numbers in the same memory, and a processor will run whatever the program counter points at.

code-runs-motor.text: If the code is right, a motor on a pin is thought to run; a pin gives about 20 mA and a motor needs hundreds, so it needs its own supply switched by a transistor or driver.

one-signal-speed-direction.text: Speed and direction are thought to come from one signal; in an H-bridge two inputs set the direction and a separate PWM signal sets the speed.

separate-supplies-no-ground.text: Two separate supplies are thought to need no connection; the grounds must be joined so the driver can read the board's signals against the same 0 V.

mah-is-strength.text: A battery's mAh is thought to be its power or strength; it is how much charge it holds, which sets how long it lasts at a given current, while the voltage is set separately.

wall-one-side.text: A box's inside width is thought to be the outside minus one wall; there is a wall on each side, so it is the outside minus two walls.

same-size-fits.text: A peg and a hole drawn the same size are thought to fit; printed holes come out smaller and pegs bigger, so a fit needs a planned clearance.

print-strength-equal.text: A printed part is thought to be equally strong every way; layers bond less well than the plastic along a layer, so parts are weaker across their layer lines.

more-infill-better.text: More infill is thought to always be better; it costs time and plastic for little strength, while extra walls add more strength for less.

edit-means-redraw.text: Changing a design is thought to mean redrawing it; in a parametric model the dimensions are linked, so changing one updates everything that depends on it.

cut-on-the-line.text: A laser is thought to cut exactly on the line; the beam burns away a width (the kerf), so cut slots come out wider and parts smaller than drawn.

looks-is-structure.text: A style sheet is thought to change what a part of a page is (big text becomes a heading); CSS changes only how it looks, and the HTML tag says what it is.

same-look-same-page.text: Two pages that look the same are thought to be the same for everyone; screen readers, search engines and phone layouts use the structure, so faked headings and lists fail them.

compound-ratios-add.text: The stage ratios of a compound gear train are thought to add; they multiply, because each stage slows down (and strengthens) a turn the stage before has already slowed.

idler-changes-ratio.text: A gear between two others (an idler) is thought to change the ratio, more for a bigger idler; its teeth cancel out, so it changes only the direction of the turn.

lever-distance-from-end.text: Distances on a lever are measured from the end of the bar; turning effects use each force's distance from the pivot.

pulley-count-pull-rope.text: The rope you pull is counted as holding the load; only the ropes holding up the moving block share it, so a rope that goes over the top block adds nothing.

stroke-equals-radius.text: A crank's stroke is thought to equal its radius; the pin goes from one side of the centre to the other, so the stroke is twice the radius.

grashof-wrong-pair.text: To check whether a four-bar linkage's crank can turn fully, the wrong two bars are added; the rule adds the shortest and the longest and compares them with the other two.

cd-moves-files.text: cd is thought to move files along with you; it only changes the folder you are working in, and mv moves files.

ls-shows-everything.text: What plain ls shows is taken to be everything in a folder; names starting with a dot are hidden and need ls -a.

rm-recycle-bin.text: rm is thought to send files to a recycle bin; in a shell, deleted files are gone, so copy first.

pipe-reads-files.text: A command after a pipe is thought to read the original file; it reads the previous command's output.

hidden-is-protected.text: A hidden (dot) file is thought to be private; anyone allowed by its permissions can list and read it, so permissions (chmod 600) protect it.

symbols-make-strong.text: Swapping letters for symbols (P@ssw0rd!) is thought to make a password strong; those swaps are on every guessing list. Length and randomness (four random words), used on one site only, make it strong.

mfa-only-important.text: A second factor is thought to be needed only on 'important' accounts; any account that can reset others or message friends is worth protecting, starting with email.

right-name-is-safe.text: A message showing a trusted name is thought to be from that person; display names can be anything, so check the address and what the message asks for.

more-data-better.text: Collecting extra data 'in case it's useful' is thought to be harmless; every item held can leak and adds to people's footprint, so collect only what the purpose needs.

https-solves-all.text: HTTPS is thought to make an app secure; it protects data on the way, not data stored or who is allowed to see it.

good-code-is-safe.text: An app with no bugs in its own code is thought to be safe; people (user weaknesses) and the code it relies on (supply chain) can still let someone in.

policy-means-anything.text: Having a privacy policy is thought to allow any use of data; the Australian Privacy Principles limit what may be collected, used and shared, policy or not.

truss-count-add.text: The members a rigid frame needs are worked out as 2 × joints + 3; the rule is members + 3 = 2 × joints (for a pin and a roller), so members = 2 × joints − 3.

every-image-pixels.text: Every picture is thought to be made of pixels, so a blocky logo needs more pixels; a vector stores shapes as numbers and is drawn again sharp at any size.

encoding-is-encryption.text: Data written in binary, hex or base64 is thought to be secret because it looks scrambled; the rule is public, so anyone can decode it. Encryption needs a secret key.

hidden-on-page-is-private.text: Something not shown on a web page (a comment, a hidden field, a script) is thought to be private; the whole page is sent to every visitor, so anyone can read its source.

wifi-password-is-https.text: A Wi-Fi password is thought to make everything sent on the network private; everyone with the password is on the network too, and past the router data crosses the internet, so only HTTPS protects it end to end.

else-always-runs.text: Both paths of an if / else run, or else runs last and covers the if.

remainder-is-divide.text: i % 2 means i divided by 2 (or a percentage), not the remainder left over.

elif-both-run.text: When an if and its elif are both true, both paths run.

for-each-is-index.text: In for c in colours, c is a place number (0, 1, 2), not the item itself.

index-starts-one.text: The first item of a list is in place 1, so the third item is colours[3].

len-is-last-index.text: The last place of a list equals its length, so a list of 8 ends at place 8.

quotes-optional.text: Text can be written without quotes: print(Hello); in fact Python reads a word with no quotes as a name, so text needs quotes.

join-adds-space.text: + puts a space between the pieces it joins; in fact it joins with nothing in between, and a space appears only if it is inside the quotes.

input-is-prompt.text: The name holds the question that input showed; in fact it holds what the person typed.

input-not-stored.text: Calling input() is enough to use the answer later; in fact the answer is lost unless a name catches it, as in name = input(...).

str-changes-in-place.text: str(n) on its own line turns n into text; in fact it makes a text copy and n stays a number.

int-reads-words.text: int can turn number words like twelve into a number; in fact int only reads digits, and anything else stops the program.

check-after-convert.text: The isdigit check can come after int; in fact the conversion runs first and crashes before the check is reached.

condition-checked-late.text: A while loop stops the moment its condition becomes false, even mid-pass; in fact the condition is checked before every pass, so the body always finishes first.

plus-equals-replaces.text: total += n puts n into total; in fact it adds n to what total already holds.

break-leaves-if.text: break leaves only the if it sits in; in fact it leaves the whole loop.

while-true-forever.text: A while True loop stops by itself when the program is done; in fact only a break ends it.

works-for-me.text: A program works if the cases that were tried work; in fact the cases that fail are the ones nobody tried, such as wrong inputs.

code-lines-show.text:
Pressing Enter in the code starts a new line on the page; in fact the browser ignores line breaks in the code, and only a new

starts a new paragraph.

ol-numbers-typed.text:
The numbers in a numbered list are typed by hand, as in
  • 1. Sprint
    • ; in fact
      numbers its items itself.

href-shows.text: The address inside href is what the page shows, or what people click; in fact only the words between and show.

attribute-anywhere.text: An attribute such as href can go after the > or in the closing tag; in fact it goes inside the opening tag.

alt-is-caption.text: alt is a caption shown under the picture, or the name of the file; in fact it describes the picture for people who cannot see it, and shows only when the picture does not.

rule-styles-one.text: A rule such as p { } styles only the first paragraph; in fact it styles every p.

class-dot-in-html.text: The dot goes in the class attribute too, as in class=".note"; in fact the dot is only in the CSS.

table-by-column.text: A table is written a column at a time; in fact it is written a row at a time, one <tr> after another.

id-repeats.text: Two elements can share an id; in fact each id names one element, and a link to a repeated id goes to the first.

hash-missing.text: href="results" jumps to the element with id results; in fact the # is needed (href="#results"), or the browser looks for a page called results.

form-sends-itself.text: Pressing a form's button saves or sends the answers by itself; in fact it needs code behind the form to do anything with them.

one-rule-only.text: An element follows only one rule, the first or the last that names it; in fact it takes the properties of every rule that matches, and a class rule beats a tag rule when they set the same property.

color-reaches-links.text: nav { color: white; } turns the links in the nav white; in fact a link keeps its own colour until a rule names the link, as in nav a { }.

space-means-both.text: nav a styles the nav and also every a; in fact the space means inside, so only links inside the nav change.

div-adds-look.text: A <div> changes how the page looks by itself; in fact it is a plain box with no look until a rule styles it.

width-includes-padding.text: width: 200px makes the whole box 200px wide, padding and border included; in fact width sets only the content, and padding and border add to it on both sides.

justify-aligns-text.text: justify-content lines up the text inside each item; in fact it places the items themselves along the row.

justify-align-swapped.text: justify-content and align-items do the same job; in fact justify-content works along the row and align-items works across it.

wrap-shrinks.text: Items in a flex row move down to a new line by themselves when there is no room; in fact without flex-wrap: wrap they squash or run off the edge.

fixed-width-fits.text: A fixed width such as 400px fits any screen; in fact it is the same size on a phone, so cards that fit a laptop overflow.

class-per-copy.text: Each copy of a card needs its own class and its own rule (.card1, .card2); in fact copies share one class, and one rule styles them all.

class-picks-wrong.text: A class rule such as .note styles every paragraph, or only the first one; in fact it styles exactly the elements marked with that class, however many.

declaration-no-semicolon.text: A declaration in a rule can run into the next one without a semicolon; in fact the missing ; makes the browser drop both.

inline-ignores-width.text: An inline box such as a span can be given a width like any other box; in fact an inline box ignores width until display: block makes it a block box.

block-full-width.text: Every box is only as wide as its words, and a div or p sits in the line like a span; in fact a block box starts a new line and takes the full width, and only an inline box stays as wide as its words.

tag-name-sets-layout.text: A tag such as nav or header decides how its contents are laid out (links in a row, sections in a column); in fact the kind of box, block or inline, decides, and a tag only names the part.

margin-gap-same.text: margin and gap do the same job, adding space outside every item; in fact margin surrounds each item, ends of the row included, and gap sits only between neighbours.

min-width-squeezes.text: Every card fits on one line however big its min-width is, or the gaps do not count; in fact min-width is a floor, so only as many cards fit as the line has room for, gaps included.

flex-parent-no-effect.text: display: flex on a list only changes the list itself, so the items stay stacked; in fact it lines up all of its children in a row.

flex-reaches-descendants.text: display: flex lines up every box inside the parent, grandchildren too; in fact only its direct children line up, and their own contents stay inside them.

tag-rule-some.text: A tag rule such as tr { } colours only the rows I want; in fact it styles every tr, and a class is what picks some of them.

inner-tag-replaces.text: A tag inside another tag replaces the outer one, or cannot be there at all; in fact the inner tag adds its look to the outer one, so the words get both.

list-tag-decides.text: The items of a list run together on one line, or become paragraphs, whatever the tag; in fact ul gives bullets, ol gives numbers, and each li starts its own line.

nested-list-beside.text: A list for one item goes after the whole list, or inside the wrong item; in fact it sits inside its own li, and shows indented under it.
